findings.title: Second `downsize` definition overrides the (from,to,w,h,opts) version
findings.body: Ruby has no overloading, so the new `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 replaces the earlier `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`. Existing callers that pass width and height separately will now have the height bound to `opts`. That raises errors or gives a wrong dimension string, and `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer or String will fail. The earlier definition is dead code and should be removed, with all callers checked.

findings.title: Downsize loop can silently fail and does not enforce the limit
findings.body: The return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is ignored. If the conversion fails, the loop retries 5 times with no effect. `tempfile.size` may also be stale or buffered, and the loop assumes the file was rewritten in place. After the loop the file may still exceed `max_image_size_kb`, and nothing re-checks it. Each iteration also runs ImageOptim, which is expensive, all inside the request's deferred job. Oversized files rely on a later size check that no longer exists on the client.

findings.title: Downsizing applies to non-image-type uploads and can break GIFs and other formats
findings.body: `downsize` uses `convert from[0]` and writes back to the same path. Animated GIFs are reduced to the first frame unless the gifsicle path is taken. The animated path only triggers when the filename matches `/\.GIF$/i` on the temp path. Temp paths may have no extension, so animation is lost. Converting in place with the same input and output path is also risky.

findings.title: Hardcoded 10MB limit ignores site settings
findings.body: The client now ignores `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` and uses 10MB for every type, attachments included. Admins who set a lower attachment limit get no client-side validation. The server only downsizes images, so oversized attachments are no longer caught early. The 413 handler has the same hardcoded value.
